Quantitative Stability, Coercivity and Uniqueness of Optimal Transport PlansThanks: 1CMAP École Polytechnique, Palaiseau, France. Email: william.ford@polytechnique.edu

William Ford1
Abstract.

For probability measures on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} supported in fixed compact sets, we prove that quadratic optimal transport plans are quantitatively stable in Wasserstein distance under perturbation of both marginal measures, assuming that one of the initial measures satisfies an upper Ahlfors regularity condition with exponent strictly greater than d−1d-1. Under the same assumption, we also prove novel quantitative stability results for optimal transport maps.

Furthermore, we prove a coercivity theorem which states that any probability measure on the product space must be quantitatively close to the set of optimal plans, if it has similar marginals and a similar transport cost to the optimal value.

Finally, we prove a quantitative uniqueness theorem which acts as a quantitative counterpart to Brenier’s theorem. The Wasserstein diameter of the set of optimal plans is controlled by the distance of one marginal measure to a regular measure for which uniqueness holds. In this way, “almost uniqueness” of optimal plans is quantified by the source measure being “almost regular”.

Examples are provided which prove that the exponents of all estimates are sharp.

Keywords: optimal transport, quantitative stability, uniqueness, coercivity, Brenier theorem

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 49Q22, 49K40, 26B05

1. Introduction

Given two probability measures ρ\rho and μ\mu on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, the quadratic optimal transport problem between ρ\rho and μ\mu is the minimisation problem

(1.1) min⁡∫ℝd×ℝdγ∈Π⁡(ρ,μ)⁡‖x−y‖2​𝑑γ​(x,y),\min_{\gamma\in\Pi(\rho,\mu)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|x-y\|^{2}\mathrm{d}\gamma(x,y),

where Π⁡(ρ,μ)\Pi(\rho,\mu) denotes the set of all transport plans between ρ\rho and μ\mu, i.e. probability measures on ℝd×ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d} with first marginal ρ\rho and second marginal μ\mu. In this paper we study the following questions:

  1. (I)

    When are optimal plans quantitatively stable under perturbation of ρ\rho and μ\mu?

  2. (II)

    When are plans with a nearly optimal cost quantitatively close to the set of optimisers?

  3. (III)

    When is the set of optimal plans quantitatively close to a singleton, i.e. when does it have small diameter?

These questions are crucial to the many applications of optimal transport, for example in machine learning and computer vision [15, 30, 5], statistics [18, 10, 16] and numerical analysis [9, 22], where one would like to quantify the errors introduced by various approximations and estimations. To respond quantitatively to the above questions we require a distance in which we will measure the perturbations of the marginals, as well as another to compare transport plans. For r∈[1,∞]r\in[1,\infty], the rr-Wasserstein distance between ρ\rho and μ\mu is given by

(1.2) Wr​(ρ,μ)=minγ∈Π⁡(ρ,μ)⁡‖x−y‖Lr​(γ),W_{r}(\rho,\mu)=\min_{\gamma\in\Pi(\rho,\mu)}\|x-y\|_{L^{r}(\gamma)},

with problem (1.1) corresponding to the case r=2r=2. We will measure perturbations in the marginal measures using Wasserstein distances on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Solutions to (1.1) are also probability measures, and will be compared instead using Wasserstein distances on ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d}.

1.1. Contributions

For a subset EE of Euclidean space, denote by 𝒫⁡(E)\mathcal{P}(E) the set of probability measures on EE. Throughout this paper we assume d≥2d\geq 2. For marginals ρ\rho and μ\mu, we denote by Γ⁡(ρ,μ)\Gamma(\rho,\mu) the set of all solutions to problem (1.1), and γρ→μ\gamma_{\rho\to\mu} will denote any optimiser to (1.1).

The four main results of this paper are stated below: stability of optimal plans under perturbation of both marginals and optimal maps with fixed source, coercivity of the objective with respect to transport plans on ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d} with arbitrary marginals, and quantitative uniqueness of solutions near a regular source measure. All the theorems are proven in the text for WqW_{q} distances between plans and LqL^{q} between maps, for any q≥1q\geq 1. In the introduction we present only the case q=2q=2 for readability. The principal assumption in all theorems is that one of the measures satisfies the following regularity condition.

Assumption 1.1.

Assume ρ∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\rho\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that for some M>0M>0 and θ∈(0,1]\theta\in(0,1],

A⁡(M,θ)A(M,\theta) ρ⁡(Bη​(x))≤M​ηd−1+θ for every ​x∈ℝd​ and ​η>0.\rho(B_{\eta}(x))\leq M\eta^{d-1+\theta}\quad\text{ for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\text{ and }\eta>0.

A foundational result in optimal transport due to Brenier and McCann [8, 32] states that if ρ\rho vanishes on all sets of Hausdorff dimension d−1d-1, then solutions to (1.1) are unique for any μ\mu, and the optimal plan is induced by a transport map, which we denote Tρ→μT_{\rho\to\mu}. Our assumption A ( M , θ ) is strictly stronger than this, and can be viewed as a quantitative form of the Brenier-McCann hypothesis.

Theorem (Bi-marginal plan stability: Theorem 4.8, Proposition 5.2).

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be compact subsets of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for d≥2d\geq 2, and let ρ0\rho_{0} be a probability measure on 𝒳\mathcal{X} satisfying A ( M , θ ) . Then for all ρ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)\rho_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}), all μ0,μ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu_{0},\mu_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}), and any γρ1→μ1∈Γ⁡(ρ1,μ1)\gamma_{\rho_{1}\to\mu_{1}}\in\Gamma(\rho_{1},\mu_{1}),

(1.3) W2​(γρ0→μ0,γρ1→μ1)≤C​(W1​(ρ0,ρ1)+W1​(μ0,μ1))θ2​(1+θ),W_{2}(\gamma_{\rho_{0}\to\mu_{0}},\gamma_{\rho_{1}\to\mu_{1}})\leq C\Big(W_{1}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})+W_{1}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1})\Big)^{\frac{\theta}{2(1+\theta)}},

for an explicit constant C⁡(𝒳,𝒴,M)>0C(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y},M)>0 given in the statement of Theorem 4.8. Moreover, the bound is sharp in exponent for all such θ\theta.

Here, by sharpness, we mean that in general, the same inequality cannot hold with a larger exponent. The example given in Proposition 5.2 is for fixed source, perturbing only the target. Thus we do not rule out the possibility of a better exponent under perturbations of the source, with fixed target.

Our second stability theorem is for optimal maps. As soon as both marginals are perturbed, a Brenier map may not exist for the new problem. We can nonetheless discuss bi-marginal stability of the gradient of the Brenier potential, which has implications for statistical estimation of transport maps; see Remark 4.7. For clarity, we state here the fixed-source version where maps remain well defined, leaving the general case to Theorem 4.6.

Theorem (Fixed source map stability: Theorem 4.6, Proposition 5.2).

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be compact subsets of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for d≥2d\geq 2, and let ρ\rho be a probability measure on 𝒳\mathcal{X} satisfying A ( M , θ ) . Then

(1.4) ∀μ0,μ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒴),‖Tρ→μ0−Tρ→μ1‖L2​(ρ)≤C​W1​(μ0,μ1)θ2​(1+θ),\forall\mu_{0},\mu_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}),\quad\|T_{\rho\to\mu_{0}}-T_{\rho\to\mu_{1}}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\leq CW_{1}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1})^{\frac{\theta}{2(1+\theta)}},

for an explicit constant C⁡(𝒳,𝒴,M)>0C(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y},M)>0 given in the statement of Theorem 4.6. Moreover, the bound is sharp in exponent for all such θ\theta.

Observe that for fixed source measure ρ\rho, and plans γρ→μi=(Id,Tρ→μi)#​ρ\gamma_{\rho\to\mu_{i}}=(\id,T_{\rho\to\mu_{i}})_{\#}\rho induced by maps Tρ→μiT_{\rho\to\mu_{i}}, i=0,1i=0,1, the coupling (Id,Tρ→μ0,Id,Tρ→μ1)#​ρ∈Π⁡(γ0,γ1)(\id,T_{\rho\to\mu_{0}},\id,T_{\rho\to\mu_{1}})_{\#}\rho\in\Pi(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}) provides the upper bound

Wq​(γρ→μ0,γρ→μ1)≤‖Tρ→μ0−Tρ→μ1‖Lq​(ρ)W_{q}(\gamma_{\rho\to\mu_{0}},\gamma_{\rho\to\mu_{1}})\leq\|T_{\rho\to\mu_{0}}-T_{\rho\to\mu_{1}}\|_{L^{q}(\rho)}

so that in this case, map stability implies plan stability with fixed source, for the same constant and exponent.

Our third theorem gives a quantitative coercivity estimate for the transport problem. It says that for the transport problem between ρ0\rho_{0} satisfying A ( M , θ ) and any μ0\mu_{0}, any transport plan γ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒳×𝒴)\gamma_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}) (not necessarily optimal between its marginals) is quantitatively close to the optimal plan γρ0→μ0\gamma_{\rho_{0}\to\mu_{0}}, under the assumption that γ1\gamma_{1} has similar marginals to ρ0\rho_{0} and μ0\mu_{0} and realises a similar transport cost ∫‖x−y‖2​d​γ1\int\|x-y\|^{2}\mathrm{d}\gamma_{1} to γρ0→μ0\gamma_{\rho_{0}\to\mu_{0}}.

Theorem (Coercivity: Theorem 4.2, Proposition 5.3).

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be compact subsets of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for d≥2d\geq 2, let ρ0\rho_{0} be a probability measure on 𝒳\mathcal{X} satisfying A ( M , θ ) , and fix any μ0∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}). Then for any γ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒳×𝒴)\gamma_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}) with marginals ρ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)\rho_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}) and μ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}),

(1.5) W2​(γ1,γρ0→μ0)≤C​(|∫‖x−y‖2​d​γ1−W22​(ρ0,μ0)|+W1​(ρ0,ρ1)+W1​(μ0,μ1))θ2​(1+θ)\quad W_{2}(\gamma_{1},\gamma_{\rho_{0}\to\mu_{0}})\leq C\left(\left|\int\|x-y\|^{2}\mathrm{d}\gamma_{1}-W_{2}^{2}(\rho_{0},\mu_{0})\right|+W_{1}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})+W_{1}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1})\right)^{\frac{\theta}{2(1+\theta)}}

for an explicit constant C⁡(𝒳,𝒴,M)>0C(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y},M)>0 given in the statement of Theorem 4.2. Moreover, the bound is sharp in exponent for all such θ\theta.

The example given in Proposition 5.3 is for fixed marginals, so that the exponent is still sharp even restricted to this case. In the text we state and prove two other coercivity theorems. Theorem 4.4 concerns transport problems where one marginal is close in Wasserstein distance to some regular measure, and coercivity holds up to an error quantified in terms of this distance. The second, Theorem 4.5, concerns the maps constructed out of the subgradients of nearly optimal potentials for the dual problem.

Our final theorem gives a bound on the diameter of the set of optimal transport plans in terms of the distance of one marginal measure to a measure satisfying A ( M , θ ) . This provides a quantification of the Brenier-McCann theorem, saying that if one marginal is close to regular then the set of optimisers is close to being a singleton, regardless of the target measure. For q∈[1,+∞)q\in[1,+\infty) and probability measures ρ\rho and μ\mu, denote the WqW_{q} diameter of the optimal set by

diamWq⁡Γ⁡(ρ,μ):=supγ0,γ1∈Γ⁡(ρ,μ)Wq​(γ0,γ1).\diam_{W_{q}}\Gamma(\rho,\mu):=\sup_{\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}\in\Gamma(\rho,\mu)}W_{q}(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}).
Theorem (Quantitative uniqueness: Theorem 3.1, Proposition 5.1).

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be compact and convex subsets of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for d≥2d\geq 2, and let ρ~\tilde{\rho} be a probability measure on 𝒳\mathcal{X} satisfying A ( M , θ ) . Then for all ρ∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)\rho\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}) and μ∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}),

(1.6) diamW2⁡Γ⁡(ρ,μ)≤C​W2​(ρ,ρ~)θ2+θ,\diam_{W_{2}}\Gamma(\rho,\mu)\leq CW_{2}(\rho,\tilde{\rho})^{\frac{\theta}{2+\theta}},

for an explicit constant C⁡(𝒳,𝒴,M)>0C(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y},M)>0 given in the statement of Theorem 3.1. Moreover, the bound is sharp in exponent for all such θ\theta.

1.2. Existing results

Simple examples in [19] involving discrete measures show that without any regularity assumptions, problem (1.1) is not quantitatively stable. OT stability literature can be divided into two categories of assumptions: local stability in the neighbourhood of a transport problem with a regular map/potential, and local stability in the neighbourhood of a transport problem with at least one regular marginal measure. All stability results in this paper are of the second type.

For the first type of result, in [23] it is proved that with fixed probability density ρ\rho and some target μ\mu, if Tρ→μT_{\rho\to\mu} is Lipschitz, then OT maps are locally quantitatively stable in L2​(ρ)L^{2}(\rho) with respect to W1W_{1} perturbations of the target μ\mu. This is generalised to bi-marginal plan stability under the same assumption in [29]. Assuming the transport from ρ0\rho_{0} to μ0\mu_{0} has a class 𝒞1,1\mathcal{C}^{1,1} Brenier potential (see (1.7) below for the definition), Li and Nochetto establish the control

∀ρ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)​∀μ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒴),W2​(γρ0→μ0,γρ1→μ1)≲(W2​(ρ0,ρ1)+W2​(μ0,μ1))12,\forall\rho_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})\forall\mu_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}),\quad W_{2}(\gamma_{\rho_{0}\to\mu_{0}},\gamma_{\rho_{1}\to\mu_{1}})\lesssim\Big(W_{2}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})+W_{2}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1})\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}},

for a constant depending on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, and the Lipschitz constant of ∇ϕρ0→μ0\nabla\phi_{\rho_{0}\to\mu_{0}}. We also mention [21] which adapts this assumption to a larger class of transport costs, as well as [31] which derives statistical results under related regularity assumptions. Unfortunately, in applications, such regularity assumptions can be difficult to verify and need not hold. OT maps are often not even continuous, let alone Lipschitz, even between regular densities.

Assuming instead that one marginal measure is regular is often more relevant to applications. Much progress has been made recently in this direction, in particular for stability of OT maps with a regular fixed source ρ\rho, under perturbation of the target μ\mu. We mention [6] for the first such result, followed by [17, 26] in which a fixed-source stability theory is developed directly for Brenier potentials – and consequently maps – using tools from functional inequalities. For 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} a bounded Lipschitz domain and ρ\rho a probability density on 𝒳\mathcal{X} bounded above and below by positive constants, they prove that for all μ0,μ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu_{0},\mu_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}),

‖ϕρ→μ0−ϕρ→μ1‖L2​(ρ)≲W1​(μ0,μ1)12 and ‖Tρ→μ0−Tρ→μ1‖L2​(ρ)≲W1​(μ0,μ1)16,\|\phi_{\rho\to\mu_{0}}-\phi_{\rho\to\mu_{1}}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\lesssim W_{1}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1})^{\frac{1}{2}}\quad\;\text{ and }\quad\;\|T_{\rho\to\mu_{0}}-T_{\rho\to\mu_{1}}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\lesssim W_{1}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1})^{\frac{1}{6}},

where the potentials are normalised by ∫𝒳ϕρ→μi​𝑑ρ=0\int_{\mathcal{X}}\phi_{\rho\to\mu_{i}}\mathrm{d}\rho=0, and the constants depend on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, 𝒴\mathcal{Y} and the upper and lower density bounds for ρ\rho. We refer the reader to the lecture notes [27] for more details on these methods. The current state of the art papers [33, 14] prove OT map and plan stability for a larger class of source measures. Notably, the support of the regular measure need not be connected and the density can vanish arbitrarily fast. In [33], Mérigot proves that for ρ\rho a bounded, compactly supported probability density on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d},

∀μ0,μ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒴),‖Tρ→μ0−Tρ→μ1‖L2​(ρ)≲W1​(μ0,μ1)14,\forall\mu_{0},\mu_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}),\quad\|T_{\rho\to\mu_{0}}-T_{\rho\to\mu_{1}}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\lesssim W_{1}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1})^{\frac{1}{4}},

for a constant depending on 𝒴\mathcal{Y} and ρ\rho. Due to the example in [28], the exponent 1/41/4 is sharp, matching the special case of our Theorem 4.6 and Proposition 5.2 when θ=1\theta=1 and q=2q=2. In [14], Cazelles, Pauwels and Portales prove that for ρ0\rho_{0} a bounded probability density on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, for all ρ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)\rho_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}) and all μ0,μ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu_{0},\mu_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}),

W2​(γρ0→μ0,γρ1→μ1)≲(W2​(ρ0,ρ1)+W2​(μ0,μ1))18,W_{2}(\gamma_{\rho_{0}\to\mu_{0}},\gamma_{\rho_{1}\to\mu_{1}})\lesssim\Big(W_{2}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})+W_{2}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1})\Big)^{\frac{1}{8}},

for a constant depending on diam⁡(𝒳)\diam(\mathcal{X}), diam⁡(𝒴)\diam(\mathcal{Y}) and ρ0\rho_{0}. Here their exponent is not sharp. Using our Theorem 4.8 with θ=1\theta=1 and q=2q=2 improves their exponent from 1/81/8 to 1/41/4, since by Jensen’s inequality W1≤W2W_{1}\leq W_{2}. Our result is still not equal to the theoretical upper bound of 1/31/3 given by Proposition 5.2. The above results are consequences of the paper [12] on the quantitative regularity of convex functions. Our techniques in this paper extend the quantitative regularity theory to allow for our new parameters θ\theta and qq.

Coercivity of problem (1.1) has also received some study. In [29], Li and Nochetto prove that any transport problem satisfying the same 𝒞1,1\mathcal{C}^{1,1} regularity assumption on a Brenier potential is coercive in a similar sense to our Theorem 4.2 presented above. In [33], Mérigot proves two coercivity results for plans and maps with respect to both dual and primal suboptimality with fixed marginals. These form the basis for our Theorem 4.5 and Theorem 4.4. We also mention [13] which proves coercivity of the distance of a plan to the subgradient of the Brenier potential with respect to the primal suboptimality gap, as well as [11, 19] which prove a strong convexity inequality for the dual problem which acts as a dual coercivity result for Brenier potentials.

The current literature on uniqueness of the primal problem is, to the best of our knowledge, only qualitative. The foundational results of Brenier and McCann [8, 32] state that if ρ\rho vanishes on all sets of Hausdorff dimension d−1d-1, then solutions to (1.1) are unique for any μ\mu, and the optimal plan is induced by a transport map. Our assumption A ( M , θ ) can be in some sense seen as a quantitative strengthening of this Brenier-McCann hypothesis. The sharp hypotheses for qualitative uniqueness have since been identified as slightly weaker. To guarantee that the optimal transport is unique and map induced for any μ\mu, it is necessary and sufficient that ρ\rho vanishes on any hypersurface which can be locally written as the graph of a difference of convex functions; see [24, 34]. For the dual OT problem, quantitative uniqueness has been recently investigated by the author, in [20]. Here almost connectedness of one marginal measure’s support implies a quantitative bound on the diameter of the set of optimal dual potentials.

1.3. Idea of the proofs

Since

12​W22​(ρ,μ)=12​∫‖x‖2​𝑑ρ​(x)+12​∫‖y‖2​𝑑μ​(y)−supγ∈Π⁡(ρ,μ)∫⟨x,y⟩​𝑑γ​(x,y),\frac{1}{2}W_{2}^{2}(\rho,\mu)=\frac{1}{2}\int\|x\|^{2}\mathrm{d}\rho(x)+\frac{1}{2}\int\|y\|^{2}\mathrm{d}\mu(y)-\sup_{\gamma\in\Pi(\rho,\mu)}\int\langle x,y\rangle\mathrm{d}\gamma(x,y),

problem (1.1) is equivalent to the maximum correlation problem. Its dual formulation is

(1.7) supγ∈Π⁡(ρ,μ)∫⟨x,y⟩​𝑑γ=infϕ​ convex∫ϕ⁡(x)​𝑑ρ​(x)+∫ϕ∗​(y)​𝑑μ​(y),\sup_{\gamma\in\Pi(\rho,\mu)}\int\langle x,y\rangle\mathrm{d}\gamma=\inf_{\phi\text{ convex}}\int\phi(x)\mathrm{d}\rho(x)+\int\phi^{*}(y)\mathrm{d}\mu(y),

where ϕ∗​(y)=supx∈ℝd⟨x,y⟩−ϕ⁡(x)\phi^{*}(y)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\langle x,y\rangle-\phi(x) denotes the Legendre transform. We call any minimiser ϕ\phi a Brenier potential. Primal and dual optimality imply that for ϕ\phi a Brenier potential and γ\gamma an optimal plan,

spt⁡γ⊂graph⁡(∂ϕ).\spt\gamma\subset\graph(\partial\phi).

The main tool used for all the results in this paper is Theorem 2.2, which proves that for q≥1q\geq 1, a measure ρ~\tilde{\rho} satisfying A ( M , θ ) , and a convex Lipschitz function ϕ:ℝd→ℝ\phi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R},

(1.8) ∀η≥0,∫𝒳diam∂ϕ(B¯η(x))qdρ~(x)≲ηθ,\forall\eta\geq 0,\quad\int_{\mathcal{X}}\diam\partial\phi(\overline{B}_{\eta}(x))^{q}\mathrm{d}\tilde{\rho}(x)\lesssim\eta^{\theta},

where here

∂ϕ⁡(B¯η​(x))=⋃z∈B¯η​(x)∂ϕ⁡(z).\partial\phi(\overline{B}_{\eta}(x))=\bigcup_{z\in\overline{B}_{\eta}(x)}\partial\phi(z).

This extends the result of [12], which proves (1.8) when q>1q>1 and ρ\rho is the Lebesgue measure and consequently for all bounded densities, i.e. ρ\rho satisfying A ( M , θ ) with θ=1\theta=1. This result should be seen as a “quantitative regularity” result for convex functions, with the integral quantity representing average local oscillation at scale η\eta.

Once we have (1.8), then the proof of Theorem 3.1, quantitative uniqueness, is direct. We sketch the argument for the W1W_{1} plan - W1W_{1} marginal bound here. Fix any two optimal plans γ0,γ1∈Γ⁡(ρ,μ)\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}\in\Gamma(\rho,\mu) and a Brenier potential ϕ\phi, and let α∈Π⁡(ρ~,ρ)\alpha\in\Pi(\tilde{\rho},\rho) be an optimal coupling for W1​(ρ~,ρ)W_{1}(\tilde{\rho},\rho). Then, for any η>0\eta>0, by choosing a coupling π∈Π⁡(γ0,γ1)\pi\in\Pi(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}) which couples mass according to the identity for the first marginal ρ\rho of each plan (see (2.8) with β∈Π⁡(ρ,ρ)\beta\in\Pi(\rho,\rho) concentrated along the diagonal),

W1​(γ0,γ1)≤\displaystyle W_{1}(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1})\leq ∫𝒳diam∂ϕ(x)dρ(x)=∫𝒳2diam∂ϕ(x)dα(x~,x)\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{X}}\diam\partial\phi(x)\mathrm{d}\rho(x)=\int_{\mathcal{X}^{2}}\diam\partial\phi(x)\mathrm{d}\alpha(\tilde{x},x)
≤\displaystyle\leq ∫{∥x~−x∥≤η}diam∂ϕ(B¯η(x~))dα(x~,x)+D𝒴α(∥x−x~∥>η)\displaystyle\int_{\{\|\tilde{x}-x\|\leq\eta\}}\diam\partial\phi(\overline{B}_{\eta}(\tilde{x}))\mathrm{d}\alpha(\tilde{x},x)+D_{\mathcal{Y}}\alpha(\|x-\tilde{x}\|>\eta)
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ηθ+W1​(ρ~,ρ)η.\displaystyle\eta^{\theta}+\frac{W_{1}(\tilde{\rho},\rho)}{\eta}.

The bound follows by choosing η=W1​(ρ~,ρ)1/(1+θ)\eta=W_{1}(\tilde{\rho},\rho)^{1/(1+\theta)}.

The stability and coercivity theorems are less direct, as we must compare two plans which do not have the same marginals, and are not, in general, concentrated on the graph of the subgradient of the same convex function. For these bounds, we also couple transport plans in a manner which is optimal for the first marginal. The main term we are left to bound in this case is a quantitative measure of the suboptimality of one plan to being in the subgradient of the other problem’s Brenier potential, of the form

∫𝒳×𝒴Gϕ0​(x,y)​d​γ1​(x,y),\int_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}}G_{\phi_{0}}(x,y)\mathrm{d}\gamma_{1}(x,y),

where Gϕ​(x,y)=ϕ⁡(x)+ϕ∗​(y)−⟨x,y⟩≥0G_{\phi}(x,y)=\phi(x)+\phi^{*}(y)-\langle x,y\rangle\geq 0 is the slackness in the Fenchel–Young inequality at (x,y)(x,y) for a convex function ϕ\phi. In the coercivity theorem, this quantity is bounded by the difference in transport costs between γ0\gamma_{0} and γ1\gamma_{1}, plus the sum of W1W_{1} differences between their marginals. In the stability theorem, this quantity is bounded directly by the W1W_{1} differences between their marginals.

2. Quantitative regularity: coupling transport plans

In the majority of settings considered in this paper, objects are invariant under translations of 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, so we may assume without loss of generality that 00 belongs to both sets. It will also cost us no loss of generality to assume they are convex since we never ask measures to have full support. We denote the radii and diameters of each set by

R𝒳=supx∈𝒳‖x‖,R𝒴=supy∈𝒴‖y‖,D𝒳=diam⁡(𝒳),D𝒴=diam⁡(𝒴).R_{\mathcal{X}}=\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\|x\|,\quad R_{\mathcal{Y}}=\sup_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\|y\|,\quad D_{\mathcal{X}}=\diam(\mathcal{X}),\quad D_{\mathcal{Y}}=\diam(\mathcal{Y}).

When 0∈𝒳∩𝒴0\in\mathcal{X}\cap\mathcal{Y}, we have R𝒳≤D𝒳R_{\mathcal{X}}\leq D_{\mathcal{X}} and R𝒴≤D𝒴R_{\mathcal{Y}}\leq D_{\mathcal{Y}}. In general, we will always assume that a pair of Brenier and dual (ϕ,ψ)(\phi,\psi) potentials is of the form

(2.1) ϕ⁡(x)=supy∈𝒴⟨x,y⟩−ψ⁡(y) and ψ⁡(y)=supx∈𝒳⟨x,y⟩−ϕ⁡(x),\phi(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\langle x,y\rangle-\psi(y)\quad\text{ and }\quad\psi(y)=\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\langle x,y\rangle-\phi(x),

rather than taking the Legendre transform with respect to all ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Every optimal potential admits ρ\rho and μ\mu a.e. representatives of this form; see [20, Appendix B] for a rigorous justification of this assumption. Consequently, ϕ\phi and ψ\psi are R𝒴R_{\mathcal{Y}} and R𝒳R_{\mathcal{X}} Lipschitz respectively, as envelopes of uniformly Lipschitz functions.

2.2. The Fenchel gap

For (x,y)∈ℝd×ℝd(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d} and a convex function ϕ:ℝd→ℝ\phi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}, denote the remainder in the Fenchel-Young inequality by

Gϕ​(x,y)=ϕ⁡(x)+ϕ∗​(y)−⟨x,y⟩≥0,G_{\phi}(x,y)=\phi(x)+\phi^{*}(y)-\langle x,y\rangle\geq 0,

where here ϕ∗​(y)=supz∈ℝd⟨z,y⟩−ϕ⁡(z)\phi^{*}(y)=\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\langle z,y\rangle-\phi(z) is the convex conjugate. Equality Gϕ​(x,y)=0G_{\phi}(x,y)=0 is equivalent to the pair (x,y)(x,y) belonging to the graph of the subgradient of ϕ\phi, i.e. y∈∂ϕ⁡(x)y\in\partial\phi(x). In [13, Lemma 1.1], Carlier proves a quantitative bound

Gϕ​(x,y)≥12​dist⁡((x,y),graph⁡(∂ϕ))2,G_{\phi}(x,y)\geq\frac{1}{2}\dist((x,y),\graph(\partial\phi))^{2},

i.e. points which almost attain equality in Fenchel-Young are quantitatively close to the set graph⁡(∂ϕ)\graph(\partial\phi). The following lemma controls the distance of a specific yy to elements of ∂ϕ⁡(x)\partial\phi(x), rather than a pair (x,y)(x,y) to graph⁡(∂ϕ)\graph(\partial\phi).

Let ϕ:ℝd→ℝ\phi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be convex. Then for any (x,y)∈ℝd×ℝd(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}, any g∈∂ϕ⁡(x)g\in\partial\phi(x), and any η>0\eta>0,

‖y−g‖≤Dη​ϕ​(x)+Gϕ​(x,y)η.\|y-g\|\leq D_{\eta}\phi(x)+\frac{G_{\phi}(x,y)}{\eta}.

ϕ⁡(x0)≥⟨x0,y1⟩−ϕ∗​(y1),ϕ∗​(y0)≥⟨x1,y0⟩−ϕ⁡(x1),\phi(x_{0})\geq\langle x_{0},y_{1}\rangle-\phi^{*}(y_{1}),\quad\phi^{*}(y_{0})\geq\langle x_{1},y_{0}\rangle-\phi(x_{1}),

=\displaystyle= −Gϕ​(x1,y1)−⟨x1−x0,y1−y0⟩.\displaystyle-G_{\phi}(x_{1},y_{1})-\langle x_{1}-x_{0},y_{1}-y_{0}\rangle.

In particular, when one takes (x1,y1)∈graph⁡(∂ϕ)(x_{1},y_{1})\in\graph(\partial\phi), Gϕ​(x1,y1)=0G_{\phi}(x_{1},y_{1})=0 so that the first term on the right vanishes. Fix any g0∈∂ϕ⁡(x0)g_{0}\in\partial\phi(x_{0}). If y0=g0y_{0}=g_{0}, the result is immediate. Otherwise choose

x1=x0+η​y0−g0‖y0−g0‖,x_{1}=x_{0}+\eta\frac{y_{0}-g_{0}}{\|y_{0}-g_{0}\|},

2.3. Coupling transport plans

To compare probability measures γ0,γ1∈𝒫⁡(ℝd×ℝd)\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}), we use the qq-Wasserstein distance on ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d} with the norm

‖(x,y)‖=(‖x‖q+‖y‖q)1q,\|(x,y)\|=\left(\|x\|^{q}+\|y\|^{q}\right)^{\frac{1}{q}},

so that

Wqq​(γ0,γ1)=infπ∈Π⁡(γ0,γ1)∫ℝ4​d‖x0−x1‖q+‖y0−y1‖q​𝑑π​(x0,y0,x1,y1).W_{q}^{q}(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1})=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1})}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4d}}\|x_{0}-x_{1}\|^{q}+\|y_{0}-y_{1}\|^{q}\mathrm{d}\pi(x_{0},y_{0},x_{1},y_{1}).

Since all norms on finite dimensional spaces are equivalent, this distance is equivalent to the Wasserstein distance induced by the Euclidean norm on ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d}, up to multiplicative constants. All our bounds hold for any q∈[1,∞)q\in[1,\infty), with an exponent that degenerates as q→∞q\to\infty. The examples given in the sharpness section indicate that in general, one cannot hope for any of our bounds to hold for q=∞q=\infty.

For ρ0,ρ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)\rho_{0},\rho_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}) and μ0,μ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu_{0},\mu_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}), two plans γi∈Π⁡(ρi,μi)\gamma_{i}\in\Pi(\rho_{i},\mu_{i}) and a coupling β∈Π⁡(ρ0,ρ1)\beta\in\Pi(\rho_{0},\rho_{1}), we denote by πβ∈Π⁡(γ0,γ1)\pi_{\beta}\in\Pi(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}) the coupling given by

(2.8) πβ​(d​x0,d​y0,d​x1,d​y1)=β⁡(d​x0,d​x1)​γ0​(d​y0∣x0)​γ1​(d​y1∣x1),\pi_{\beta}(\mathrm{d}x_{0},\mathrm{d}y_{0},\mathrm{d}x_{1},\mathrm{d}y_{1})=\beta(\mathrm{d}x_{0},\mathrm{d}x_{1})\gamma_{0}(\mathrm{d}y_{0}\mid x_{0})\gamma_{1}(\mathrm{d}y_{1}\mid x_{1}),

where γi(⋅∣xi)\gamma_{i}(\cdot\mid x_{i}) denotes the disintegration of γi\gamma_{i} at xix_{i}. We will use the coupling πβ∈Π⁡(γ0,γ1)\pi_{\beta}\in\Pi(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}) as a competitor for the minimisation problem Wq​(γ0,γ1)W_{q}(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}), controlling its transport cost in terms of our objects of interest. In particular,

Wqq​(γ0,γ1)≤\displaystyle W_{q}^{q}(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1})\leq ∫ℝ4​d‖x0−x1‖q+‖y0−y1‖q​d​πβ\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4d}}\|x_{0}-x_{1}\|^{q}+\|y_{0}-y_{1}\|^{q}\mathrm{d}\pi_{\beta}
=\displaystyle= ∫ℝ2​d‖x0−x1‖q​𝑑β+∫ℝ4​d‖y0−y1‖q​d​πβ.\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}\|x_{0}-x_{1}\|^{q}\mathrm{d}\beta+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4d}}\|y_{0}-y_{1}\|^{q}\mathrm{d}\pi_{\beta}.

Choosing β∈Π⁡(ρ0,ρ1)\beta\in\Pi(\rho_{0},\rho_{1}) optimal for some rr-Wasserstein distance, the first term is easily controllable in terms of Wr​(ρ0,ρ1)W_{r}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1}). The majority of our work will be spent controlling the second term. Observe that when ρ=ρ0=ρ1\rho=\rho_{0}=\rho_{1} and the γi\gamma_{i} are induced by maps TiT_{i}, then for β\beta the identity coupling,

πβ=(Id,T0,Id,T1)#​ρ,∫ℝ4​d‖y0−y1‖q​d​πβ=‖T0−T1‖Lq​(ρ)q.\pi_{\beta}=(\id,T_{0},\id,T_{1})_{\#}\rho,\quad\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4d}}\|y_{0}-y_{1}\|^{q}\mathrm{d}\pi_{\beta}=\|T_{0}-T_{1}\|_{L^{q}(\rho)}^{q}.

The below lemma provides the general framework for all the bounds in this paper. The first bound considers when both plans are concentrated on the same subgradient, and the second when only one is.

Lemma 2.5 (Coupling transport plans).

Then for any α∈Π⁡(ρ~,ρ0)\alpha\in\Pi(\tilde{\rho},\rho_{0}) and β∈Π⁡(ρ0,ρ1)\beta\in\Pi(\rho_{0},\rho_{1}) and η,s≥0\eta,s\geq 0,

∫(𝒳×𝒴)2‖y0−y1‖q​d​πβ≤\displaystyle\int_{(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^{2}}\|y_{0}-y_{1}\|^{q}\mathrm{d}\pi_{\beta}\leq D𝒴q−1​(∫(𝒳×𝒴)2Ds​ϕ​(x0)​d​πβ+1s​∫(𝒳×𝒴)2Gϕ​(x0,y1)​d​πβ).\displaystyle D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{q-1}\left(\int_{(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^{2}}D_{s}\phi(x_{0})\mathrm{d}\pi_{\beta}+\frac{1}{s}\int_{(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^{2}}G_{\phi}(x_{0},y_{1})\mathrm{d}\pi_{\beta}\right).

3. Quantitative uniqueness: plans on a common subgradient

In this section we prove two theorems regarding the comparison of transport plans concentrated on the subgradient of the same convex function. The first, quantitative uniqueness, compares plans with the same marginals, when one marginal is close to regular. The second compares a plan with a regular first marginal to another plan with potentially different marginals. Although, by the triangle inequality, the second implies the first (with a larger constant), we prefer to prove the two results separately to isolate the proof mechanisms involved.

3.1. Quantitative uniqueness

Theorem 3.1 (Quantitative uniqueness).

Let q∈[1,∞)q\in[1,\infty) and r∈[1,∞]r\in[1,\infty], and let 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be compact and convex subsets of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for d≥2d\geq 2. Let ρ~\tilde{\rho} be a probability measure on 𝒳\mathcal{X} satisfying A ( M , θ ) . Then for all ρ∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)\rho\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}) and μ∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}),

(3.1) diamWq⁡Γ⁡(ρ,μ)≤C​Wr​(ρ,ρ~)ν,\diam_{W_{q}}\Gamma(\rho,\mu)\leq CW_{r}(\rho,\tilde{\rho})^{\nu},

where ν∈(0,1]\nu\in(0,1] is given by

ν={r​θq⁡(r+θ)r<∞θqr=∞,\nu=\begin{cases}\frac{r\theta}{q(r+\theta)}&r<\infty\\ \frac{\theta}{q}&r=\infty,\end{cases}

and C=D𝒴​(cd​M​D𝒳d−1+θ+1)1/q​D𝒳−ν>0C=D_{\mathcal{Y}}\left(c_{d}MD_{\mathcal{X}}^{d-1+\theta}+1\right)^{1/q}D_{\mathcal{X}}^{-\nu}>0.

Proof.

Fix two optimal plans γ0,γ1∈Γ⁡(ρ,μ)\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}\in\Gamma(\rho,\mu). If Wr​(ρ,ρ~)=0W_{r}(\rho,\tilde{\rho})=0 then ρ=ρ~\rho=\tilde{\rho} and the result holds by the Brenier-McCann theorem, so assume that Wr​(ρ,ρ~)>0W_{r}(\rho,\tilde{\rho})>0, with α\alpha the optimal coupling between them. Fix a Brenier potential ϕ\phi for the transport from ρ\rho to μ\mu. We apply Lemma 2.5 with β\beta the identity coupling and s=0s=0:

∫‖y0−y1‖q​d​πβ≤D𝒴q−1​∫𝒳Dη​ϕ​(x~)​𝑑ρ~​(x~)+D𝒴q​α​(‖x~−x0‖>η).\int\|y_{0}-y_{1}\|^{q}\mathrm{d}\pi_{\beta}\leq D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{q-1}\int_{\mathcal{X}}D_{\eta}\phi(\tilde{x})\mathrm{d}\tilde{\rho}(\tilde{x})+D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{q}\alpha(\|\tilde{x}-x_{0}\|>\eta).

We apply Theorem 2.2 and a Markov bound. For η>0\eta>0,

∫‖y0−y1‖q​d​πβ≤D𝒴q​(cd​M​D𝒳d−1+θ​(ηD𝒳)θ+Wrr​(ρ,ρ~)ηr).\int\|y_{0}-y_{1}\|^{q}\mathrm{d}\pi_{\beta}\leq D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{q}\left(c_{d}MD_{\mathcal{X}}^{d-1+\theta}\left(\frac{\eta}{D_{\mathcal{X}}}\right)^{\theta}+\frac{W_{r}^{r}(\rho,\tilde{\rho})}{\eta^{r}}\right).

We balance the terms containing η\eta, choosing

(ηD𝒳)θ=Wrr​(ρ,ρ~)ηr, so that η=(Wrr​(ρ,ρ~)​D𝒳θ)1/(r+θ).\left(\frac{\eta}{D_{\mathcal{X}}}\right)^{\theta}=\frac{W_{r}^{r}(\rho,\tilde{\rho})}{\eta^{r}},\quad\text{ so that }\quad\eta=\left(W_{r}^{r}(\rho,\tilde{\rho})D_{\mathcal{X}}^{\theta}\right)^{1/(r+\theta)}.

Consequently,

(3.2) ∫‖y0−y1‖q​d​πβ≤D𝒴q​(cd​M​D𝒳d−1+θ+1)​D𝒳−r​θr+θ​Wr​(ρ,ρ~)r​θr+θ.\int\|y_{0}-y_{1}\|^{q}\mathrm{d}\pi_{\beta}\leq D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{q}\left(c_{d}MD_{\mathcal{X}}^{d-1+\theta}+1\right)D_{\mathcal{X}}^{-\frac{r\theta}{r+\theta}}W_{r}(\rho,\tilde{\rho})^{\frac{r\theta}{r+\theta}}.

This is the claimed bound. For r=+∞r=+\infty, the proof is the same, choosing η=W∞​(ρ,ρ~)\eta=W_{\infty}(\rho,\tilde{\rho}) without needing any Markov bound. ∎

Remark 3.2 (Uniformity of constant in qq and rr and θ\theta).

The statements of the theorems in the introduction claim the existence of a constant depending on only 𝒳\mathcal{X}, 𝒴\mathcal{Y} and MM, and a priori, the above constant

C=D𝒴​(cd​M​D𝒳d−1+θ+1)1/q​D𝒳−νC=D_{\mathcal{Y}}\left(c_{d}MD_{\mathcal{X}}^{d-1+\theta}+1\right)^{1/q}D_{\mathcal{X}}^{-\nu}

does not satisfy this. Since any constant which holds for all measures on 𝒳′\mathcal{X}^{\prime} also holds for all measures on 𝒳⊂𝒳′\mathcal{X}\subset\mathcal{X}^{\prime}, with D𝒳≤D𝒳′D_{\mathcal{X}}\leq D_{\mathcal{X}}^{\prime}, we can freely replace instances of D𝒳D_{\mathcal{X}} by max⁡(1,D𝒳)\max(1,D_{\mathcal{X}}); then max⁡(1,D𝒳)−ν≤1\max(1,D_{\mathcal{X}})^{-\nu}\leq 1 and max⁡(1,D𝒳)d−1+θ≤max⁡(1,D𝒳)d\max(1,D_{\mathcal{X}})^{d-1+\theta}\leq\max(1,D_{\mathcal{X}})^{d}. Furthermore, since the expression inside the qqth root is larger than 11, we can bound this by the same term without the qqth root. Thus a choice of constant depending only on 𝒳,𝒴\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y} and MM is given by

C=D𝒴​(1+cd​M​max⁡(1,D𝒳)d).C=D_{\mathcal{Y}}(1+c_{d}M\max(1,D_{\mathcal{X}})^{d}).

The same principle applies to all the other theorems using similar calculations.

3.2. Plans on the same subgradient with different marginals

The above result uses the α\alpha coupling in Lemma 2.5. If instead we use the β\beta coupling, we can arrive at the following theorem of independent interest, which generalises a result of [14] to compare transport plans in the same subgradient with different marginals. We improve their exponent and give a general Wq−WrW_{q}-W_{r} bound rather than W2−W2W_{2}-W_{2}. Our exponent is proven sharp in Proposition 5.1. We use this theorem in the Appendix to give an alternative proof of stability for the optimal transport plans.

Theorem 3.3 (Same subgradient plan control).

Let q≥1q\geq 1 and r∈[1,∞]r\in[1,\infty], let 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be compact and convex subsets of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for d≥2d\geq 2, and let ρ0\rho_{0} be a probability measure on 𝒳\mathcal{X} satisfying A ( M , θ ) . Let ϕ:ℝd→ℝ\phi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be convex with ∂ϕ⁡(ℝd)⊂𝒴\partial\phi(\mathbb{R}^{d})\subset\mathcal{Y}, and set γ0=(Id,∇ϕ)#​ρ0\gamma_{0}=(\id,\nabla\phi)_{\#}\rho_{0}. Then for any γ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒳×𝒴)\gamma_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}) satisfying spt⁡γ1⊂graph⁡(∂ϕ)\spt\gamma_{1}\subset\graph(\partial\phi) with first marginal ρ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)\rho_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}),

Wq​(γ0,γ1)≤C​Wr​(ρ0,ρ1)ν,W_{q}(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1})\leq CW_{r}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})^{\nu},

where ν∈(0,1]\nu\in(0,1] is given by

ν={r​θq⁡(r+θ)r<∞θqr=∞,\nu=\begin{cases}\frac{r\theta}{q(r+\theta)}&r<\infty\\ \frac{\theta}{q}&r=\infty,\end{cases}

and Cq=D𝒳q⁡(1−ν)+D𝒴q​(1+cd​M​D𝒳d−1+θ)​D𝒳−q​νC^{q}=D_{\mathcal{X}}^{q(1-\nu)}+D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{q}(1+c_{d}MD_{\mathcal{X}}^{d-1+\theta})D_{\mathcal{X}}^{-q\nu}.

Proof.

If Wr​(ρ0,ρ1)=0W_{r}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})=0, then ρ0=ρ1\rho_{0}=\rho_{1}, and differentiability of ϕ\phi ρ0\rho_{0}-almost everywhere implies γ0=γ1\gamma_{0}=\gamma_{1}, so assume that Wr​(ρ0,ρ1)>0W_{r}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})>0.

We apply Lemma 2.5 with ρ~=ρ0\tilde{\rho}=\rho_{0}, ρ0=ρ0\rho_{0}=\rho_{0}, ρ1=ρ1\rho_{1}=\rho_{1}, α∈Π⁡(ρ0,ρ0)\alpha\in\Pi(\rho_{0},\rho_{0}) the identity plan, β\beta optimal for Wr​(ρ0,ρ1)W_{r}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1}), and η=0\eta=0. Then for all s≥0s\geq 0,

Wqq​(γ0,γ1)≤\displaystyle W_{q}^{q}(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1})\leq ∫𝒳2‖x0−x1‖q​𝑑β​(x0,x1)\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{X}^{2}}\|x_{0}-x_{1}\|^{q}\mathrm{d}\beta(x_{0},x_{1})
+∫𝒳Dsqϕ(x0)dρ0(x0)+D𝒴qβ(∥x0−x1∥>s).\displaystyle+\int_{\mathcal{X}}D_{s}^{q}\phi(x_{0})\mathrm{d}\rho_{0}(x_{0})+D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{q}\beta(\|x_{0}-x_{1}\|>s).

For the last two terms, Theorem 2.2 and Markov’s inequality give, for finite rr and 0<s0<s,

∫𝒳Ds​ϕ​(x0)q​d​ρ0​(x0)+D𝒴q​β​(‖x0−x1‖>s)\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{X}}D_{s}\phi(x_{0})^{q}\mathrm{d}\rho_{0}(x_{0})+D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{q}\beta(\|x_{0}-x_{1}\|>s)
≤D𝒴q​(cd​M​D𝒳d−1​sθ+Wrr​(ρ0,ρ1)sr).\displaystyle\leq D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{q}\left(c_{d}MD_{\mathcal{X}}^{d-1}s^{\theta}+\frac{W_{r}^{r}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})}{s^{r}}\right).

As in the quantitative uniqueness theorem, we choose

(sD𝒳)θ=Wrr​(ρ0,ρ1)sr, so that s=(Wrr​(ρ0,ρ1)​D𝒳θ)1/(r+θ),\left(\frac{s}{D_{\mathcal{X}}}\right)^{\theta}=\frac{W_{r}^{r}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})}{s^{r}},\quad\text{ so that }\quad s=\left(W_{r}^{r}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})D_{\mathcal{X}}^{\theta}\right)^{1/(r+\theta)},

which, substituting, gives

which, after combining with (3.3), gives the result. ∎

4. Coercivity and stability: plans close to a common subgradient

In this section, we prove two coercivity theorems for plans, showcasing two different types of bound. In principle, one could create a combined coercivity theorem containing both, but for readability, we prefer to present each idea separately. We then prove a coercivity theorem for maps with respect to dual suboptimality, followed by the two main stability theorems for maps and plans.

4.1. Coercivity for plans with arbitrary marginals

We note that unlike every other theorem in this paper, the constants in the following theorem are not translation invariant with respect to the marginals, as the suboptimality gap between plans with different marginals is not translation invariant. Indeed, for any a∈ℝda\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and γ0,γ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒳×𝒴)\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}), define

γia=(x+a,y)#​γi∈𝒫⁡((𝒳+a)×𝒴).\gamma_{i}^{a}=(x+a,y)_{\#}\gamma_{i}\in\mathcal{P}((\mathcal{X}+a)\times\mathcal{Y}).

Then

∫(𝒳+a)×𝒴⟨x,y⟩​d​(γ1a−γ0a)=\displaystyle\int_{(\mathcal{X}+a)\times\mathcal{Y}}\langle x,y\rangle\mathrm{d}(\gamma_{1}^{a}-\gamma_{0}^{a})= ∫𝒳×𝒴⟨x+a,y⟩​d​(γ1−γ0)\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}}\langle x+a,y\rangle\mathrm{d}(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{0})
=\displaystyle= ∫𝒳×𝒴⟨x,y⟩​d​(γ1−γ0)+⟨a,∫𝒴y​d​(μ1−μ0)⟩,\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}}\langle x,y\rangle\mathrm{d}(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{0})+\big\langle a,\int_{\mathcal{Y}}y\mathrm{d}(\mu_{1}-\mu_{0})\big\rangle,

which can be made to take any value by varying aa, if μ1\mu_{1} and μ0\mu_{0} do not have the same barycentre. Thus some constants here will be given in terms of R𝒳R_{\mathcal{X}} and R𝒴R_{\mathcal{Y}}. We will control the mixed Fenchel deficit appearing in Lemma 2.5 using the following lemma.

Lemma 4.1.

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be compact convex subsets of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for d≥2d\geq 2, and let ρ0,ρ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)\rho_{0},\rho_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}) and μ0,μ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu_{0},\mu_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}). Fix ϕ\phi a Brenier potential between ρ0\rho_{0} and μ0\mu_{0}. Then for any γ0∈Γ⁡(ρ0,μ0)\gamma_{0}\in\Gamma(\rho_{0},\mu_{0}) optimal and any γ1∈Π⁡(ρ1,μ1)\gamma_{1}\in\Pi(\rho_{1},\mu_{1}),

∫(𝒳×𝒴)2Gϕ​(x0,y1)​d​πβ≤\displaystyle\int_{(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^{2}}G_{\phi}(x_{0},y_{1})\mathrm{d}\pi_{\beta}\leq |∫𝒳×𝒴⟨x,y⟩​d​(γ0−γ1)|+R𝒴​W1​(ρ0,ρ1)+R𝒳​W1​(μ0,μ1),\displaystyle\left|\int_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}}\langle x,y\rangle\mathrm{d}(\gamma_{0}-\gamma_{1})\right|+R_{\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})+R_{\mathcal{X}}W_{1}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1}),

where πβ\pi_{\beta} is the coupling defined in (2.8), with β\beta chosen optimal for W1​(ρ0,ρ1)W_{1}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1}).

Proof.

Denote ψ=ϕ∗\psi=\phi^{*}. We have

∫(𝒳×𝒴)2Gϕ​(x0,y1)​d​πβ=\displaystyle\int_{(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^{2}}G_{\phi}(x_{0},y_{1})\mathrm{d}\pi_{\beta}= ∫ϕ​d​ρ0+∫ψ​d​μ1−∫⟨x0,y1⟩​d​πβ\displaystyle\int\phi\mathrm{d}\rho_{0}+\int\psi\mathrm{d}\mu_{1}-\int\langle x_{0},y_{1}\rangle\mathrm{d}\pi_{\beta}
=\displaystyle= ∫ϕ​d​ρ0+∫ψ​d​μ0−∫⟨x1,y1⟩​d​γ1\displaystyle\int\phi\mathrm{d}\rho_{0}+\int\psi\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}-\int\langle x_{1},y_{1}\rangle\mathrm{d}\gamma_{1}
+∫⟨x1−x0,y1⟩dπβ+∫ψd(μ1−μ0).\displaystyle+\int\langle x_{1}-x_{0},y_{1}\rangle\mathrm{d}\pi_{\beta}+\int\psi\mathrm{d}(\mu_{1}-\mu_{0}).

By optimality, ∫ϕ​d​ρ0+∫ψ​d​μ0=∫⟨x,y⟩​d​γ0\int\phi\mathrm{d}\rho_{0}+\int\psi\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}=\int\langle x,y\rangle\mathrm{d}\gamma_{0}. By the Cauchy-Schwarz and Kantorovich-Rubinstein inequalities,

∫⟨x1−x0,y1⟩​d​πβ≤R𝒴​∫‖x0−x1‖​𝑑β,∫ψ​d​(μ1−μ0)≤R𝒳​W1​(μ0,μ1),\int\langle x_{1}-x_{0},y_{1}\rangle\mathrm{d}\pi_{\beta}\leq R_{\mathcal{Y}}\int\|x_{0}-x_{1}\|\mathrm{d}\beta,\qquad\int\psi\mathrm{d}(\mu_{1}-\mu_{0})\leq R_{\mathcal{X}}W_{1}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1}),

which completes the proof. ∎

Theorem 4.2 (Arbitrary marginal coercivity).

Let q≥1q\geq 1, and let 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be compact and convex subsets of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for d≥2d\geq 2. Let ρ0\rho_{0} be a probability measure on 𝒳\mathcal{X} satisfying A ( M , θ ) , let μ0∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}), and denote by γ0\gamma_{0} the unique optimal plan between them. Then for any ρ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)\rho_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}), μ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}) and any plan γ1∈Π⁡(ρ1,μ1)\gamma_{1}\in\Pi(\rho_{1},\mu_{1}),

Wq​(γ0,γ1)≤C​(|∫𝒳×𝒴⟨x,y⟩​d​(γ0−γ1)|+R𝒴​W1​(ρ0,ρ1)+R𝒳​W1​(μ0,μ1))θq⁡(1+θ)W_{q}(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1})\leq C\left(\left|\int_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}}\langle x,y\rangle\mathrm{d}(\gamma_{0}-\gamma_{1})\right|+R_{\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})+R_{\mathcal{X}}W_{1}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1})\right)^{\frac{\theta}{q(1+\theta)}}

4.2. Approximate coercivity with an almost regular source measure

The second plan coercivity theorem concerns the transport problem where one marginal ρ\rho satisfies A ( M , θ ) only approximately, similar to the quantitative uniqueness theorem. In this case, we prove that for any μ\mu, the ρ→μ\rho\to\mu transport problem is coercive up to an error given in terms of Wr​(ρ,ρ~)W_{r}(\rho,\tilde{\rho}). While for r=1r=1 this theorem is implied by the above coercivity theorem combined with the stability theorem, for other rr the error exponent here is sharper. Since we only treat the fixed marginal case, we are once again in the setting where constants are translation invariant, so can be stated in terms of the diameters.

(4.2) 𝒦ρ,μ​(ψ)=∫𝒳ψ∗​𝑑ρ+∫𝒴ψ​𝑑μ,\mathcal{K}_{\rho,\mu}(\psi)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\psi^{*}\mathrm{d}\rho+\int_{\mathcal{Y}}\psi\mathrm{d}\mu,

4.4. Stability of optimal maps

The following theorem provides a stability bound for optimal transport maps with respect to perturbation of both marginals, again extending a result [33, Theorem 3.3] to general exponents qq and θ\theta, as well as improving the numerical constant.

A priori, there are some issues with regard to what one means by a bi-marginal stability result for optimal transport maps. In general, as soon as both marginals are perturbed, a Brenier map Tρ1→μ1T_{\rho_{1}\to\mu_{1}} need not exist, since ∂ϕρ1→μ1\partial\phi_{\rho_{1}\to\mu_{1}} may be multivalued on a set of positive ρ1\rho_{1} measure. Here we compare the gradients of the Brenier potentials with respect to Lq​(ρ0)L^{q}(\rho_{0}), using that the gradient of any convex function is well defined ρ0\rho_{0} almost everywhere.

Nonetheless, given a Brenier potential for the transport from ρ1\rho_{1} to μ1\mu_{1}, there is no canonical choice for what values it should take outside the support of ρ1\rho_{1}, and so the gradients of two different Brenier potentials, although they are both well defined, might differ on a set of positive ρ0\rho_{0} measure. The below theorem applies to any Brenier potential which satisfies (2.1).

Theorem 4.6 (Bi-marginal Brenier gradient stability).

Let q∈[1,+∞)q\in[1,+\infty), let 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be compact subsets of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and let ρ0∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)\rho_{0}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}) satisfy A ( M , θ ) . Then for all ρ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)\rho_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}) and μ0,μ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu_{0},\mu_{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}), and Brenier potentials ϕρi→μi\phi_{\rho_{i}\to\mu_{i}}

‖∇ϕρ0→μ0−∇ϕρ1→μ1‖Lq​(ρ0)q≤C​(D𝒴​W1​(ρ0,ρ1)+D𝒳​W1​(μ0,μ1))θ1+θ\|\nabla\phi_{\rho_{0}\to\mu_{0}}-\nabla\phi_{\rho_{1}\to\mu_{1}}\|_{L^{q}(\rho_{0})}^{q}\leq C\Big(D_{\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})+D_{\mathcal{X}}W_{1}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1})\Big)^{\frac{\theta}{1+\theta}}

where CC is the constant in Theorem 4.5.

Proof.

Let (ϕ0,ψ0)(\phi_{0},\psi_{0}) and (ϕ1,ψ1)(\phi_{1},\psi_{1}) be pairs of optimal potentials for the transport between ρi\rho_{i} and μi\mu_{i} respectively. We apply the dual coercivity Theorem 4.5 to the ρ0,μ0\rho_{0},\mu_{0} problem, using that (ϕ1,ψ1)(\phi_{1},\psi_{1}) is a competitor to the dual 𝒦ρ0,μ0\mathcal{K}_{\rho_{0},\mu_{0}}. Thus

(4.3) ‖∇ϕρ0→μ0−∇ϕρ1→μ1‖Lq​(ρ0)q≤C​(∫ϕ1​d​ρ0+∫ψ1​d​μ0−∫ϕ0​d​ρ0−∫ψ0​d​μ0)θ1+θ.\|\nabla\phi_{\rho_{0}\to\mu_{0}}-\nabla\phi_{\rho_{1}\to\mu_{1}}\|_{L^{q}(\rho_{0})}^{q}\leq C\left(\int\phi_{1}\mathrm{d}\rho_{0}+\int\psi_{1}\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}-\int\phi_{0}\mathrm{d}\rho_{0}-\int\psi_{0}\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}\right)^{\frac{\theta}{1+\theta}}.

Adding the second dual suboptimality gap

∫ϕ0​d​ρ1+∫ψ0​d​μ1−∫ϕ1​d​ρ1−∫ψ1​d​μ1≥0\int\phi_{0}\mathrm{d}\rho_{1}+\int\psi_{0}\mathrm{d}\mu_{1}-\int\phi_{1}\mathrm{d}\rho_{1}-\int\psi_{1}\mathrm{d}\mu_{1}\geq 0

to the right hand side of (4.3) inside the bracket,

‖∇ϕρ0→μ0−∇ϕρ1→μ1‖Lq​(ρ0)q≤C​(∫(ϕ1−ϕ0)​d​(ρ0−ρ1)+∫(ψ1−ψ0)​d​(μ0−μ1))θ1+θ.\|\nabla\phi_{\rho_{0}\to\mu_{0}}-\nabla\phi_{\rho_{1}\to\mu_{1}}\|_{L^{q}(\rho_{0})}^{q}\leq C\left(\int(\phi_{1}-\phi_{0})\mathrm{d}(\rho_{0}-\rho_{1})+\int(\psi_{1}-\psi_{0})\mathrm{d}(\mu_{0}-\mu_{1})\right)^{\frac{\theta}{1+\theta}}.

Since ∇ϕi⊂𝒴\nabla\phi_{i}\subset\mathcal{Y} and ∇ψi⊂𝒳\nabla\psi_{i}\subset\mathcal{X} for i=0,1i=0,1, then the functions ϕ1−ϕ0\phi_{1}-\phi_{0} and ψ1−ψ0\psi_{1}-\psi_{0} are D𝒴D_{\mathcal{Y}} and D𝒳D_{\mathcal{X}} Lipschitz respectively, so the result follows by Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality. ∎

Remark 4.7 (Interpretation for statistical estimation of transport maps).

The theorem has the following implications for approximation of transport maps. It says that if one can solve the dual problem for ρ1,μ1\rho_{1},\mu_{1} to get some Brenier potential ϕρ1→μ1\phi_{\rho_{1}\to\mu_{1}} defined on all 𝒳\mathcal{X}, then ∇ϕρ1→μ1\nabla\phi_{\rho_{1}\to\mu_{1}} is a good approximator in Lq​(ρ0)L^{q}(\rho_{0}) for the transport map Tρ0→μ0=∇ϕρ0→μ0T_{\rho_{0}\to\mu_{0}}=\nabla\phi_{\rho_{0}\to\mu_{0}}. This means that a map constructed out of the gradient of the Brenier potential ϕρ1→μ1\phi_{\rho_{1}\to\mu_{1}} will, on average, send samples from ρ0\rho_{0} to a point near the image of the true optimal map Tρ0→μ0T_{\rho_{0}\to\mu_{0}}.

The fixed source stability of optimal transport maps presented in the introduction is a direct consequence of the above version by taking ρ0=ρ1\rho_{0}=\rho_{1}, since Tρ→μi=∇ϕρ→μiT_{\rho\to\mu_{i}}=\nabla\phi_{\rho\to\mu_{i}}.

4.5. Stability of optimal plans

We now prove the bi-marginal stability of optimal transport plans with respect to perturbation of both marginals. This is a relatively direct consequence of Theorem 4.2. In the appendix, we present a second proof of this theorem using Theorem 4.6 and Theorem 3.3.

Theorem 4.8 (Bi-marginal stability of optimal plans).

Let q∈[1,+∞)q\in[1,+\infty), and let 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be compact convex subsets of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for d≥2d\geq 2. Wq​(γρ0→μ0,γρ1→μ1)≤C​(W1​(ρ0,ρ1)+W1​(μ0,μ1))θq⁡(1+θ),W_{q}(\gamma_{\rho_{0}\to\mu_{0}},\gamma_{\rho_{1}\to\mu_{1}})\leq C\Big(W_{1}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})+W_{1}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1})\Big)^{\frac{\theta}{q(1+\theta)}},

Proof.

Since all the quantities in the theorem are invariant under translation of source and target domains, we can assume without loss of generality that 0∈𝒳∩𝒴0\in\mathcal{X}\cap\mathcal{Y}. We apply the arbitrary marginal coercivity theorem, Theorem 4.2, with γi=γρi→μi\gamma_{i}=\gamma_{\rho_{i}\to\mu_{i}}, so that

and we replaced the instances of R𝒳R_{\mathcal{X}} and R𝒴R_{\mathcal{Y}} by D𝒳D_{\mathcal{X}} and D𝒴D_{\mathcal{Y}}, since 0∈𝒳∩𝒴0\in\mathcal{X}\cap\mathcal{Y}. where we used the suboptimality of (ϕ1,ψ1)(\phi_{1},\psi_{1}) in the ρ0\rho_{0} to μ0\mu_{0} dual problem, followed by Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality. 5. Sharpness

In this section we provide two examples which prove that the four main theorems are sharp in exponent, in the sense that the same bound cannot hold with a better exponent. The first example provides sharpness for quantitative uniqueness as well as the same subgradient plan control, while the second provides sharpness for the stability and coercivity of plans, as well as stability of maps. The second example is heavily based on the example given in [28], which corresponds to the case θ=1\theta=1.

5.1. Sharpness for uniqueness

In general, it is challenging to ascertain a lower bound on Wq​(γ0,γ1)W_{q}(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}), since often the optimal coupling between the plans is not clear. This is in contrast to lower bounding a distance between maps ‖T0−T1‖Lq​(ρ)\|T_{0}-T_{1}\|_{L^{q}(\rho)}, where as soon as the optimal map is known explicitly, the distance can be calculated. For this first example, it is sufficient for us to use the crude bound

Wqq​(γ0,γ1)≥∫dist⁡((x,y),spt⁡γ0)q​d​γ1​(x,y),W_{q}^{q}(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1})\geq\int\dist((x,y),\spt\gamma_{0})^{q}\mathrm{d}\gamma_{1}(x,y),

as the expression on the right is more easily calculable. This bound holds since, at best, every point in spt⁡γ1\spt\gamma_{1} is coupled with its closest point to spt⁡γ0\spt\gamma_{0}.

5.2. Sharpness for stability of maps and plans

In our second example, we cannot use the crude support distance lower bound, and Wq​(γ0,γ1)W_{q}(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}) is instead lower bounded by a form of measure theoretic pigeonhole principle. Roughly speaking, we show that although for every point in spt⁡γ0\spt\gamma_{0} there is a nearby point in spt⁡γ1\spt\gamma_{1}, the mass given locally to certain regions of the product space by each plan is different, and so any coupling between the two plans must couple a certain amount of mass across a long distance.

The example shows that even for the fixed source estimate, the plan stability exponent is optimal. This automatically implies the same upper bound on the exponent for the distance between maps, since Wq​(γρ→μ0,γρ→μ1)≤‖Tρ→μ0−Tρ→μ1‖Lq​(ρ)W_{q}(\gamma_{\rho\to\mu_{0}},\gamma_{\rho\to\mu_{1}})\leq\|T_{\rho\to\mu_{0}}-T_{\rho\to\mu_{1}}\|_{L^{q}(\rho)}. Thus although we do not explicitly calculate the map distance, this example also gives sharpness of the map stability, Theorem 4.6.

5.3. Sharpness for coercivity

The above example can be adapted to show that the coercivity theorems, Theorems 4.2 and 4.4, are also sharp in exponent. The general form of this is already sharp as a consequence of the sharpness for stability with r=1r=1. The example below uses fixed marginals, establishing that the exponent in terms of the suboptimality deficit is also sharp.

Proposition 5.3.

Let d≥2d\geq 2 and θ∈(0,1]\theta\in(0,1]. Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be compact convex sets in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with nonempty interior. There exists a probability measure ρ\rho on 𝒳\mathcal{X} satisfying A ( M , θ ) for some M>0M>0, a measure μ∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}), and transport plans (γi)i∈ℕ∈Π⁡(ρ,μ)(\gamma_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\in\Pi(\rho,\mu) such that for any q∈[1,+∞)q\in[1,+\infty) and

α>θq⁡(1+θ),\alpha>\frac{\theta}{q(1+\theta)},

it holds that

(5.4) lim supi→∞Wq​(γρ→μ,γi)(∫⟨x,y⟩​d​(γρ→μ−γi))α=∞.\limsup_{i\to\infty}\frac{W_{q}(\gamma_{\rho\to\mu},\gamma_{i})}{\left(\int\langle x,y\rangle\mathrm{d}(\gamma_{\rho\to\mu}-\gamma_{i})\right)^{\alpha}}=\infty.

Consequently the exponents in Theorems 4.2 and 4.4 are sharp.

Proof.

We use the same construction as for the stability, taking the same ρ\rho, and μ=μ0\mu=\mu_{0}. The optimal plan is induced by the map T0T_{0} already calculated. For a candidate suboptimal plan, we choose γi∈Π⁡(ρ,μ)\gamma_{i}\in\Pi(\rho,\mu) induced by the (non-optimal) map

Ti​(x)={T0​(x)x∉Ri+∪Ri−yi+x∈Ri+yi−x∈Ri−.T_{i}(x)=\begin{cases}T_{0}(x)&x\notin R_{i}^{+}\cup R_{i}^{-}\\ y_{i}^{+}&x\in R_{i}^{+}\\ y_{i}^{-}&x\in R_{i}^{-}.\end{cases}

Using the same pigeonhole argument lower bound as for the stability, we deduce

Wq​(γρ→μ,γi)=2​ai​σi1/q,W_{q}(\gamma_{\rho\to\mu},\gamma_{i})=2a_{i}\sigma_{i}^{1/q},

where the equality is a consequence of the upper bound by ‖T0−Ti‖Lq​(ρ)=2​ai​σi1/q\|T_{0}-T_{i}\|_{L^{q}(\rho)}=2a_{i}\sigma_{i}^{1/q}. To compute the excess transport cost, we compute

Δi:=∫‖Ti​(x)−x‖2−‖T0​(x)−x‖2​𝑑ρ​(x)=∫‖x−y‖2​d​(γi−γρ→μ)=2​∫⟨x,y⟩​d​(γρ→μ−γi),\Delta_{i}:=\int\|T_{i}(x)-x\|^{2}-\|T_{0}(x)-x\|^{2}\mathrm{d}\rho(x)=\int\|x-y\|^{2}\mathrm{d}(\gamma_{i}-\gamma_{\rho\to\mu})=2\int\langle x,y\rangle\mathrm{d}(\gamma_{\rho\to\mu}-\gamma_{i}),

since the marginals are equal. The maps are equal on Ri+∩{x2≥0}R_{i}^{+}\cap\{x_{2}\geq 0\} and Ri−∩{x2≤0}R_{i}^{-}\cap\{x_{2}\leq 0\}, and for x∈Ri+∩{x2≤0}x\in R_{i}^{+}\cap\{x_{2}\leq 0\} we have

‖Ti​(x)−x‖2−‖T0​(x)−x‖2=\displaystyle\|T_{i}(x)-x\|^{2}-\|T_{0}(x)-x\|^{2}= ‖x−yi+‖2−‖x−yi−‖2\displaystyle\|x-y_{i}^{+}\|^{2}-\|x-y_{i}^{-}\|^{2}
=\displaystyle= (ai−x2)2−(ai+x2)2=4​ai​|x2|\displaystyle(a_{i}-x_{2})^{2}-(a_{i}+x_{2})^{2}=4a_{i}|x_{2}|

with the value on Ri−∩{x2≥0}R_{i}^{-}\cap\{x_{2}\geq 0\} equal by symmetry. Consequently,

Δi=2ai∫Ri+∪Ri−|x2|dρ(x)=4​ai​liZθ∫−hi/2hi/2|x2|θdx2=4Zθ​(1+θ)​2θailihi1+θ.\Delta_{i}=2a_{i}\int_{R_{i}^{+}\cup R_{i}^{-}}|x_{2}|\mathrm{d}\rho(x)=\frac{4a_{i}l_{i}}{Z_{\theta}}\int_{-h_{i}/2}^{h_{i}/2}|x_{2}|^{\theta}\mathrm{d}x_{2}=\frac{4}{Z_{\theta}(1+\theta)2^{\theta}}a_{i}l_{i}h_{i}^{1+\theta}.

Finally, for α>0\alpha>0 and the same sequences as the previous proposition,

Wq​(γρ→μ,γi)Δiα=Cρ,θ,q,α​ai(q+1q−2​α)​hi(θq−α⁡(1+θ))\frac{W_{q}(\gamma_{\rho\to\mu},\gamma_{i})}{\Delta_{i}^{\alpha}}=C_{\rho,\theta,q,\alpha}a_{i}^{\left(\frac{q+1}{q}-2\alpha\right)}h_{i}^{\left(\frac{\theta}{q}-\alpha(1+\theta)\right)}

so that the sequence only remains bounded as i→∞i\to\infty when

θq−α⁡(1+θ)≥0⟹α≤θq⁡(1+θ).\frac{\theta}{q}-\alpha(1+\theta)\geq 0\implies\alpha\leq\frac{\theta}{q(1+\theta)}.

Thus Theorems 4.2 and 4.4 are also sharp in exponent when comparing plans with fixed marginals as required. ∎

Appendix A Further estimates and an alternative proof of stability

In this appendix, we present a second proof of Theorem 4.8, which uses the same subgradient plan comparison theorem, Theorem 3.3. We also prove a strong convexity result for the Kantorovich functional, generalising the result of [33] to allow for our exponents qq and θ\theta.

A.1. An alternative proof of Theorem 4.8: bi-marginal plan stability

We combine the same subgradient control with the bi-marginal map stability Theorem 4.6. This recovers the exponent of Theorem 4.8, with a possibly different constant. Let ρ0\rho_{0} satisfy A ( M , θ ) and let ϕi\phi_{i} be Brenier potentials for the ρi→μi\rho_{i}\to\mu_{i} transport problems, chosen as in (2.1). Set γ^=(Id,∇ϕ1)#​ρ0\hat{\gamma}=(\id,\nabla\phi_{1})_{\#}\rho_{0}. Then by the same subgradient control Theorem 3.3, with r=1r=1,

Wq​(γρ1→μ1,γ^)≤C​W1​(ρ0,ρ1)θq⁡(1+θ)W_{q}(\gamma_{\rho_{1}\to\mu_{1}},\hat{\gamma})\leq CW_{1}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})^{\frac{\theta}{q(1+\theta)}}

for some C⁡(𝒳,𝒴,θ,q,M)>0C(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y},\theta,q,M)>0. By coupling the two graph plans through their common source and applying Theorem 4.6,

Wq​(γρ0→μ0,γ^)\displaystyle W_{q}(\gamma_{\rho_{0}\to\mu_{0}},\hat{\gamma}) ≤‖∇ϕ0−∇ϕ1‖Lq​(ρ0)\displaystyle\leq\|\nabla\phi_{0}-\nabla\phi_{1}\|_{L^{q}(\rho_{0})}
≤C​(W1​(ρ0,ρ1)+W1​(μ0,μ1))θq⁡(1+θ)\displaystyle\leq C\Big(W_{1}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})+W_{1}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1})\Big)^{\frac{\theta}{q(1+\theta)}}

for some C⁡(𝒳,𝒴,θ,q,M)>0C(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y},\theta,q,M)>0. Bi-marginal plan stability then follows by the triangle inequality.

A.2. Strong convexity of the Kantorovich functional via the Jensen divergence

We study the strong convexity properties of the Kantorovich functional, defined for compact sets 𝒳,𝒴\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y} as 𝒦ρ:𝒞0​(𝒴)→ℝ\mathcal{K}_{\rho}:\mathcal{C}^{0}(\mathcal{Y})\to\mathbb{R},

𝒦ρ​(ψ)=∫𝒳ψ∗​(x)​𝑑ρ​(x).\mathcal{K}_{\rho}(\psi)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\psi^{*}(x)\mathrm{d}\rho(x).

𝒦ρ\mathcal{K}_{\rho} is convex and 1-Lipschitz in the uniform norm, and when ρ\rho satisfies A ( M , θ ) , 𝒦ρ\mathcal{K}_{\rho} is everywhere Gâteaux differentiable, with

∇𝒦ρ(ψ)=−∇ψ#∗ρ.\nabla\mathcal{K}_{\rho}(\psi)=-\nabla\psi^{*}_{\#}\rho.

For more details see [27]. We measure the strong convexity of 𝒦ρ\mathcal{K}_{\rho} using the Jensen divergence Jρ:𝒞0​(𝒴)×𝒞0​(𝒴)→ℝJ_{\rho}:\mathcal{C}^{0}(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{C}^{0}(\mathcal{Y})\to\mathbb{R},

Jρ​(ψ0,ψ1):=12​(𝒦ρ​(ψ0)+𝒦ρ​(ψ1))−𝒦ρ​(12​(ψ0+ψ1)).J_{\rho}(\psi_{0},\psi_{1}):=\frac{1}{2}\Big(\mathcal{K}_{\rho}(\psi_{0})+\mathcal{K}_{\rho}(\psi_{1})\Big)-\mathcal{K}_{\rho}\Big(\frac{1}{2}(\psi_{0}+\psi_{1})\Big).

The following theorem generalises [33, Theorem 2.2], which corresponds to our result for θ=1\theta=1 and q=2q=2.

Let q∈[1,+∞)q\in[1,+\infty), let 𝒳,𝒴⊂ℝd\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be compact and convex for d≥2d\geq 2, and let ρ\rho be a probability measure on 𝒳\mathcal{X} satisfying A ( M , θ ) . Then for all ψ0,ψ1∈𝒞0​(𝒴)\psi_{0},\psi_{1}\in\mathcal{C}^{0}(\mathcal{Y}),

C=θ​(1+θ)−1+θθ​4−1+θθ​(kq​D𝒴q+θ⁡(q−1)​cd​M​D𝒳d−1)−1θC=\theta(1+\theta)^{-\frac{1+\theta}{\theta}}4^{-\frac{1+\theta}{\theta}}\left(k_{q}D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{q+\theta(q-1)}c_{d}MD_{\mathcal{X}}^{d-1}\right)^{-\frac{1}{\theta}}
